To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

patients who are more difficult to treat, have more prior hospitalizations and episodes of incompetence and lower GAF scores, are diagnosed with a psychotic or cognitive disorder, are prescribed more medications, have lower IQs, and have more special observations are more likely to remain incompetent and to have a longer stay.

incompetent defendants with a history of prior hospitalization and incompetence, lower level charges, a psychotic and cognitive disorders, and who are prescribed multiple medications are more likely to be nonrestorable, and incompetent defendants with low IQs, low GAF scores, and who spend more time on special observations have longer competency restoration LOS.

patients who are not restored are those who have more prior hospitalizations and episodes of incompetence; are charged with less serious offenses; have more psychotic, cognitive, and mood disorders; are prescribed more medications; and have lower GAF scores.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characteristics of restorable and non restorable incompetent patients and the factors that predict competency restorability.
understanding how to best treat and restore incompetent defendants.
the identification and description of the characteristics of incompetent and nonrestorable patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

incompetent patients who are nonrestorable have more prior psychiatric hospitalizations and criminal justice involvement, more psychotic disorders and lower IQs, are prescribed more medications, have lower GAF scores, are more often on special observations, have lower charges, and have more previous episodes of incompetence.
the nonrestorables were more severely mentally ill, had more extensive histories of mental health problems, had lower IQs, and had more extensive histories with the criminal justice system.
the most predictive factor for restoration of competency was the presence of a psychotic disorder, followed by a cognitive disorder and then a substance abuse disorder.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
patients who are more difficult to restore are more likely to be nonrestorable.
the nonrestorables had a longer and more complicated history of mental illness and were less likely to be diagnosed with substance use disorders.
nonrestorable defendants have more psychiatric and criminal histories and are more impaired than restorable defendants and that the severity of their impairments is associated with longer LOS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no single predictor that can be used to determine whether a defendant is restorable or not.
nonrestorability is associated with multiple variables, including demographic, criminological, and historical psychiatric variables, and current treatment factors.

nonrestorable defendants tend to have a history of prior hospitalizations, prior incarcerations, and a history of prior incompetence, which is not surprising given the high base rate of these variables in this population.
